generatedProse.concept-context: In your subject, the first answer is rarely the best one. Instead of starting over with a new prompt, you make a move on the one you have. You can ask the tool to expand a point, add context from your module, go deeper on a comparison, check for bias, or verify a claim. Each move builds on the last, so the dialogue gets sharper rather than resetting.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who each get a bland first answer from an AI tool about a theory they are studying.

{{learner-a}} is not satisfied, so {{learner-a}} deletes the chat and writes a brand-new prompt from scratch. The second answer is just as general as the first. {{learner-a}} tries a third time, rewording the question again, and keeps losing the thread. Nothing builds, because every attempt starts over.

{{learner-b}} keeps the dialogue going. First {{learner-b}} asks the tool to go deeper and compare two versions of the theory. Then {{learner-b}} adds context: use examples from my module. Next {{learner-b}} asks what the answer leaves out, and finally asks which claims to verify against the reading. Each move sharpens the last, and the answer becomes genuinely useful.

Both started from the same weak answer. Only {{learner-b}} improved it with deliberate moves instead of starting again.
generatedProse.summary: Prompting is a dialogue, not a single exchange. When the first answer falls short, you make a move - expand, add context, go deeper, check bias, or verify - rather than start over. You can now combine these moves to enrich an answer, design a sequence that deepens rather than resets, and choose the moves that fit your own task. Next come the techniques that turn these moves into real understanding.

check.body: In the worked example, why did the second student's answer end up more useful than the first's?

items.text: They improved the first answer with deliberate moves instead of starting a new prompt each time.
They used a more powerful AI tool for the task.
They accepted the first answer and moved on quickly.
They asked the same question in three slightly different ways.

feedback.correct: That's right. Making moves on one dialogue builds on what came before; restarting throws it away.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the second student did with the first answer rather than around it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The second student made deliberate moves - deeper, more context, checking and verifying - on one dialogue. A different tool, quick acceptance, or rewording from scratch were not the point.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
